This will probably come as no shock at all, but that's a pretty misleading statement. The DoD, not the Army, is Red Hat's biggest customer. The Army taps DoD resources, yes, but so does the Air Force, the Marines, the Navy, and the Coast Guard. The problem with saying that any one of those, or even the DoD itself, is Red Hat's "biggest customer" in any way that implies such a relationship could be leveraged, though, is that none of this is on a single contract; it's hundreds or even thousands of individual contracts, many of them with their own Red Hat license agreements.

Everyone gets DoD pricing, of course, but it's not like the Military Health Systems project could come along and boast that they're going to have the Nuclear Preparedness project pull funding if such-and-such wasn't done. Even if there was that level of cooperation between the projects, and believe me there isn't, nobody short of the Joint Chiefs has the power to make that kind of call. The "shouting fire in a crowded theatre" quote was made by Oliver Wendell Holmes in the Schenck case. Schenck was a socialist activist who was passing out flyers to people on the street. The flyers argued that the US should not be involved in World War I and that the military draft was a form of slavery. He was arrested and charged with sedition. His conviction was upheld arguing that passing out anti-war pamphlets was a "clear and present danger" identical to shouting fire in a crowded theatre.

So realize that when people say shouting fire is an action not a speech, they are talking about "actions" such as being a non-violent peace advocate passing out pamphlets to people arguing against war. That's the sort of "action" we mean here.

Also one should be aware US vs Schenck is now a dead letter case that was overturned decades ago in Brandenburg v. Ohio which ruled that even explicitly advocating violence is protected free speech, unless the speech is "likely" to produce "imminent lawless action". Schenck is not cited as a legal precedent or valid ruling any more.

The important exceptional case is where the person who is being incited might reasonably be expected to to follow the call to act. This case breaks into two sub-cases: where the person being incited is mentally incapable, in which case the person calling for the act is guilty, and where the person or people being incited are in a highly emotionally charged environment. In this second case it is temporarily acceptable to censor or arrest someone making such a call for action, until the person or people are no longer emotionally irrational.
